## Warmup {.inverse .middle}

Turn the `french_fries` data from wide format into a long format with variables `type` and `rating`. 
  
```{r your turn to work on the french fries data, echo=FALSE}
head(french_fries)
```

`r countdown::countdown(5)`

## What would you like to find out about the french fries data set? {.inverse}

Go to menti.com at 2979 2396 and let us know!

![](images/mentimeter_qr_code.png){width="30%"}



## What would we like to know?
  
- Is the design complete?
- Are replicates like each other?
- How do the ratings on the different scales differ?
- Are raters giving different scores on average?
- Do ratings change over the weeks?
  
Each of these questions involves different summaries of the data.


## Pivot french fries to long
  
```{r put french fries in long form}
ff_long <- french_fries |> 
  pivot_longer(potato:painty, names_to = "type", values_to = "rating")


head(ff_long)
```



## Pivot long to wide {.r-fit-text .smaller}

::: columns
::: {.column width="30%"}
![](images/tidyr-pivoting.gif){width="100%"}
:::
::: {.column  width="70%"}
Examples: 

- Are replicates like each other?
    - compare rep 1 to rep 2 values
- How do the ratings on the different scales differ?
    - compare ratings across scales
- Are raters giving different scores on average? 
    - compare ratings across raters
- Do ratings change over the weeks?
    - compare ratings week-by-week

:::
:::



## Pivot to wide form {.smaller}
  
`tidyr`'s **pivot_wider** function creates variables with comparable values

Long form:
  
```{r original form}
knitr::kable(head(ff_long, 4))
```

## Pivot to wide form {.smaller}

`tidyr`'s **pivot_wider** function creates variables with comparable values

Wide form: 
```{r spread it back into wide form}
french_fries_weeks <- ff_long |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = "time", values_from = "rating")
```

```{r}
kable(head(french_fries_weeks,3))
```


## Pivot to wide form {.smaller}
::: columns
::: {.column width="80%"}
```{r spread}
head(french_fries_weeks)
```
::: 
::: {.column width="20%"}
![[Tidyr cheatsheet](https://github.com/rstudio/cheatsheets/blob/main/tidyr.pdf)](images/tidyr-cheatsheet.png)
:::
:::

`pivot_wider`:

- creates a new column for each value of the variable in `names_from`
- fills values in using the variable in `values_from`

## Your turn: Are the replicates similar? {.inverse}

- Plot the replicates against each other using a scatterplot. 
- First, convert the data into long form
- Get the replicates spread into separate columns by replicate. 

`r countdown::countdown(5)`

```{r solution to do the replicates look like each other, echo=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
ff.s <- ff_long |> pivot_wider(names_from=rep, values_from=rating)
ggplot(data=ff.s, aes(x=`1`, y=`2`)) + geom_point() +
  theme(aspect.ratio=1) 
ggplot(data=ff.s, aes(x=`1`, y=`2`)) + geom_point() +
  theme(aspect.ratio=1) + 
  xlab("Rep 1") + ylab("Rep 2") + facet_wrap(~type, ncol=5)
```


## Are ratings similar on different scales?
  
- Scales: potato-y, buttery, grassy, rancid and painty?
- Pivot into long form, plot with `facet_...(~scale)`. 

```{r ratings on the different scales}
ff.m <- french_fries |> 
pivot_longer(-(time:rep), names_to="type", values_to="rating")
```
```{r, echo = F, include = T}
head(ff.m)
```



## Are ratings similar across different scales?
  
```{r, fig.height=2, fig.width=8}
ggplot(data=ff.m, aes(x=rating)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth=2) + 
  facet_wrap(~type, ncol=5) 
```


## Side-by-side boxplots

```{r side-by-Side boxplots, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
ggplot(data=ff.m, aes(x=type, y=rating, fill=type)) + 
  geom_boxplot()
```


## Your turn: Correlation b/w scales? {.inverse}

- Create a wide form of the data by type of scale. 

- `cor` allows you to create a correlation matrix.    
Run `?cor` to look up how to get rid of `NA` values in the result. 

- Draw a scatterplot of two scales with the highest (positive or negative) correlation value.

`r countdown::countdown(7)`

```{r solution to whether scales look like each other, echo=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
ff.scales <- ff_long |> pivot_wider(names_from=type, values_from=rating)

cor(ff.scales[,5:9], use="pairwise.complete")

ggplot(data=ff.scales, aes(x=potato, y=buttery)) + geom_point() +
  theme(aspect.ratio=1) 
```



## Ratings by week
Use the long form of the data and plot:

```{r ratings by week, fig.width=8, fig.height=3, message = F, warning = F}
ff.m$time <- as.numeric(ff.m$time)
ggplot(data=ff.m, aes(x=time, y=rating, colour=type)) + 
geom_point(size=.75) +
geom_smooth() +
facet_wrap(~type, ncol = 5)
```


## Your turn: Ratings by time & scale? {.inverse .middle}

- Find a linear model describing the average rating by week (time) and type of scale as shown below.
- Which form of the dataset should we use?
- Challenge: can you plot the fitted lines from the model?

```{r ratings by week again, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=2.5, message = F, warning = F}
ff.m$time <- as.numeric(ff.m$time)
ggplot(data=ff.m, aes(x=time, y=rating, colour=type)) + 
geom_point(size=.75) +
geom_smooth() +
facet_wrap(~type, ncol = 5)
```

`r countdown::countdown(7)`

```{r solution to model, echo=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
# long model is fine to use for a single model:

model <- lm(rating ~ type*time-1, data = ff_long)

ggplot(data=ff.m, aes(x=time, y=rating, colour=type)) + 
geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE, aes(colour = type))
```
